analysis.one_liner: Bans commodity index funds from letting pure speculators bet on oil and gas prices.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Agriculture Committee without a hearing or vote, despite 26 House members—every one a Democrat—backing it.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for commodity index funds to take money from investors who have no actual stake in energy markets—people betting purely on price movements in crude oil, natural gas, and fuels made from them. The bill's findings argue that this kind of 'index trading' reversed the balance of the futures market, so speculators now hold 70% of contracts, and may have added as much as $1 to the price of a gallon of gasoline. Its goal was to push those investors out of energy markets and bring gas prices down for drivers.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and households that buy gasoline, heating oil, and natural gas, if the bill's premise is right that index-fund speculation inflates energy prices. Businesses that hedge real energy purchases—airlines, truckers, farmers buying fuel—would keep their legal hedging position under the bill.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful for a commodity index fund to trade in energy commodities, accept investments, or hold energy positions if any investor in the fund lacks a bona fide hedging position in energy [S2][S3].

The bill's own findings state that speculators went from 30% to 70% of open commodity futures contracts, driven almost entirely by commodity index funds, and that excessive speculation may have added nearly $1.00 per gallon to the price of gasoline [S3].
Physical hedgers—businesses with a real stake in energy prices—keep full access to the market; only investors with no hedging position in any energy commodity are excluded [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Commodity index funds and the Wall Street banks that run them would lose a large pool of fee income; institutional investors like pension funds and universities that use index funds to diversify would lose a vehicle the bill says had over $160 billion in long positions in U.S. markets [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Index funds, swap dealers, and institutional investors

drawbacks.text: The bill's core premise—that index speculation added up to $1 per gallon—is stated in the bill's findings [S3], but the link between index trading and oil prices has long been disputed among economists; if the premise is wrong, the ban raises prices for no consumer benefit.

The ban would force pension funds and universities out of an investment vehicle the bill itself says held over $160 billion in long positions, costing them a tool for diversifying retirement and endowment portfolios [S3].
Removing speculators could shrink market liquidity, which in some conditions can make prices jump more, not less, when buyers and sellers are thin.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If the bill's premise is right, drivers gain real money at the pump and the cost falls on financial firms and their institutional clients, not ordinary people. But the premise is contested: independent economists have disagreed for years about how much index speculation moves oil prices, so the bill bet consumer relief on a mechanism that was not settled fact. The two-year phase-out for existing holdings was a genuine attempt to soften the disruption.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and its subcommittee on commodities, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Markey introduced the bill on April 27, 2012, with seven original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture [S1][S5].
Twenty-five additional Democrats cosponsored the bill [S4].
On May 10, 2012, it was referred to the Subcommittee on General Farm Commodities and Risk Management, the subcommittee that oversees commodity futures law, and no further action was taken [S5].
The bill's final action was the subcommittee referral; the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, with the bill never reported out of committee or voted on [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Commodity index funds, the dealers who manage them, and their institutional investors kept their positions and fee income; nothing changed for energy consumers either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Commodity index funds and their institutional clients

for.name: Rep. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban commodity index funds from energy speculation

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over commodity futures law
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 27, 2012, referred it to its commodities subcommittee on May 10, and took no further action before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All 25 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-run Agriculture Committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Commodity index funds and swap dealers
industries.note: The bill would bar these funds from energy markets entirely if any investor lacks a hedging position, ending a fee business the bill says had over $160 billion in long positions. Their business model profits from price exposure that the bill's findings say inflates costs for consumers.

The bill identifies these as major index-fund investors and would cut off their access to energy index products as a diversification tool. They are investors, not price-setters, so their loss is a side effect rather than the bill's target.

industries.industry: Physical energy hedgers (fuel buyers and producers with bona fide hedging positions)
industries.note: Businesses with real hedging positions in energy keep full market access, preserving the hedging function of the futures market for those with actual price exposure.
